query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight HEAs, service‐temperature exposure triggers Mg segregation that leads to the nucleation of Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates. When these precipitates remain finely dispersed—especially along grain boundaries—they preserve or promote the formation of a continuous, protective oxide layer (by maintaining an optimal local chemistry) that retains high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance. However, if the precipitation kinetics allow coarsening and a more complete depletion of Mg from the matrix, then the protective oxide scale is compromised, leading to a loss of corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A non‐equilibrium, metastable solid-solution alloy with a homogeneous distribution of Mg and other constituent elements.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to service-relevant thermal conditions (e.g., moderate to high temperatures over controlled time intervals) and compare with unexposed samples.
generation.conditions: Thermal ageing in atmospheres relevant to high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 850–1050 °C or as appropriate for the intended application) and subsequent corrosive testing (e.g., exposure to acidic environments such as H2SO4 solution).
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that form primarily at grain boundaries and intra-granular sites.
generation.mechanism: Upon thermal exposure, Mg atoms segregate and nucleate (and subsequently coarsen) as discrete intermetallic phases. Fine, nanoscale precipitates sequester Mg locally without depleting the neighboring matrix, thereby sustaining the formation of a protective oxide (possibly incorporating Mg-oxides) that enhances resistance to corrosion and high-temperature oxidation. Conversely, when kinetics favor coarser precipitate growth, the matrix is left Mg-depleted, hindering the development of a continuous, protective scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that develop and maintain a fine, dispersed Mg-rich precipitate network will show improved or retained corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state, whereas samples in which the intermetallics coarsen will exhibit degraded resistance.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, non-equilibrium metastable solid-solution state of the Mg-containing HEA.
generation.boundary: The transition between service conditions that sustain fine precipitation kinetics versus those that enable rapid coarsening; this boundary is defined by a critical combination of temperature and exposure duration beyond which the matrix Mg is depleted.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of Mg segregation and precipitate coarsening, the detailed intermetallic compositions, and the precise temperature-time boundaries remain to be quantified with further experimental work.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a batch of Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples and divide them into two groups. Subject one group to controlled thermal ageing at varying temperatures and durations that span the anticipated service regime. Retain the other group in the as-cast (metastable) state. Conduct microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM with EDS mapping) to quantify the formation, size, and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Simultaneously, perform high-temperature oxidation measurements (via thermogravimetric analysis and oxide scale imaging) and corrosion tests (electrochemical tests in an acidic environment).
measurements: Precipitate size, density, and distribution (TEM/SEM, EDS mapping)
Oxide scale uniformity and thickness (TGA, SEM)
Corrosion current densities and potentials (electrochemical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal exposure does not lead to measurable Mg segregation and formation of intermetallic precipitates, or if variations in precipitate morphology do not correlate with systematic changes in oxidation and corrosion resistance compared to the baseline, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties

Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
